questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.sub_topic: First meeting of the Constituent Assembly
questions.question: The Constituent Assembly met for the first time on:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9 December 1946
Why: The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946.
Why not the others: (C) 13 December 1946 is when Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution. (A) is Independence Day. (B) is when the Constitution was adopted.
Key point: The Assembly's meetings were open to the public, and newspapers reported its debates.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.question: Francis Buchanan, whose reports describe the Rajmahal hills and the people living there, was:
options: A) A physician in the Bengal Medical Service who carried out surveys for the Company
B) A missionary who set up schools and churches among the Santhals of the Damin-i-Koh
C) The Governor-General who introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal in 1793
D) A Bengali zamindar who led the opposition to the Company's revenue policy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A physician in the Bengal Medical Service who carried out surveys for the Company
Why: Buchanan was a physician in the Bengal Medical Service who carried out detailed surveys for the East India Company.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) do not describe him. Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement.
Key point: Buchanan observed the land with an eye to the Company's commercial interests, so his reports must be read critically.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Sufi saint)
(A) Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti
(B) Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya
(C) Shaikh Fariduddin Ganj-i Shakar
(D) Shaikh Salim Chishti

List-II (Place of the dargah)
(I) Ajmer
(II) Fatehpur Sikri
(III) Delhi
(IV) Ajodhan (Pakistan)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Muinuddin Chishti's dargah is at Ajmer (I), Nizamuddin Auliya's at Delhi (III), Fariduddin Ganj-i Shakar's at Ajodhan (IV) and Salim Chishti's at Fatehpur Sikri (II).
Why not the others: (B) swaps Ajmer and Delhi. (C) swaps Ajodhan and Fatehpur Sikri. (D) swaps Delhi and Ajodhan.
Key point: Akbar visited the Ajmer dargah many times, and he built Fatehpur Sikri near the hospice of Salim Chishti.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) The Kheda satyagraha
(B) The Quit India Movement
(C) The Salt March to Dandi
(D) The launch of Non-Cooperation
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (D), (C), (B)
Why: Kheda came in 1918, Non-Cooperation was launched in 1920, the Salt March took place in 1930, and Quit India was launched in 1942.
Why not the others: (B) puts Non-Cooperation before Kheda. (C) puts the Salt March before Non-Cooperation. (D) puts Quit India before the Salt March.
Key point: Gandhi's three great mass movements were Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: After the British recaptured Delhi, Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and sentenced to life imprisonment. He was sent to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Rangoon
Why: Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon, where he died in November 1862.
Why not the others: (B) The Andamans were used for other rebels. (A) and (C) were not his place of exile.
Key point: The rebels had made the last Mughal emperor their nominal leader because the Mughal name still carried legitimacy.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question: In Puranic Hinduism, Vishnu came to be worshipped through his many forms, or avatars. The tradition recognised:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ten avatars
Why: The Vaishnava tradition recognised ten avatars, forms that the deity was believed to take to save the world when it was threatened.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are the wrong number. (D) is the number of Jaina tirthankaras.
Key point: Different avatars were popular in different regions, which helped local deities be identified with Vishnu.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question: As constitutional adviser, ____ prepared a series of papers on the political systems of other countries to help the Assembly in its work.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) B.N. Rau
Why: B.N. Rau, the constitutional adviser, prepared papers on the constitutions of other countries.
Why not the others: (A) S.N. Mukherjee was the chief draughtsman. (B) Munshi and (D) Alladi Krishnaswamy Aiyar were lawyer members of the Assembly.
Key point: Rau, Mukherjee and Ambedkar formed the technical core behind the Constitution's text.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) Krishnadeva Raya comes to the throne
(B) Colin Mackenzie surveys the ruins at Hampi
(C) The empire is founded by Harihara and Bukka
(D) Vijayanagara's defeat at Rakshasi-Tangadi (Talikota)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Why: The empire was founded in 1336, Krishnadeva Raya came to the throne in 1509, the defeat at Talikota came in 1565, and Mackenzie surveyed Hampi in 1800.
Why not the others: (A) puts Talikota before Krishnadeva Raya. (C) puts Krishnadeva Raya before the founding. (D) puts Mackenzie before Talikota.
Key point: Krishnadeva Raya's reign (1509–29) was the empire's high point.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: The project of preparing a critical edition of the Mahabharata, which compared Sanskrit manuscripts from different parts of the subcontinent, was started in 1919 under the leadership of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) V.S. Sukthankar
Why: The project began in 1919 under V.S. Sukthankar. It took 47 years and ran to over 13,000 pages.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are other historians. None of them led the critical edition.
Key point: The critical edition showed both common elements and many regional variations across the manuscripts.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Magadha between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE:
(A) Magadha became the most powerful of the mahajanapadas.
(B) Agriculture was very productive there, and iron mines were easy to reach.
(C) Its early capital was Rajagaha, but the capital was shifted to Pataliputra in the fourth century BCE.
(D) Magadha was governed by a gana or sangha, with no kings.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) follow NCERT. Magadha rose because of fertile land, iron mines, elephants from its forests and easy river transport. Rajagaha was its first capital and Pataliputra its later one.
Why not the others: (D) is false. Magadha was ruled by ambitious kings such as Bimbisara, Ajatasattu and Mahapadma Nanda. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Rajagaha means "house of the king". It was a fortified settlement among hills.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: Identify the incorrectly matched pair from the Mahabharata:
options: A) Gandhari – mother of the Kauravas
B) Kunti – mother of the Pandavas
C) Duryodhana – eldest of the Pandavas
D) Drona – teacher of both Kauravas and Pandavas
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Duryodhana – eldest of the Pandavas
Why: Duryodhana was the eldest of the Kauravas. The eldest Pandava was Yudhishthira.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correctly matched.
Key point: Both the Kauravas and the Pandavas belonged to the ruling Kuru family. The war arose from rival claims to land and power.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Ryotwari settlement
(B) Limitation Law of 1859
(C) Lathyal
(D) Jotedar

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A rule that loan bonds would be valid for only three years
(II) Revenue settled directly with the cultivator, as in the Bombay Deccan
(III) Rich peasant who controlled large areas of land in a Bengal village
(IV) A strongman with a lathi, employed by a zamindar
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: The Ryotwari settlement was made directly with ryots (II). The Limitation Law limited loan bonds to three years (I). Lathyals were zamindars' lathi-wielding strongmen (IV), and jotedars were rich Bengal peasants (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two. (C) swaps the law and the lathyal. (D) swaps the lathyal and the jotedar.
Key point: Moneylenders got round the Limitation Law by making ryots sign a new bond every three years.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: In Sanskrit texts of the period, people such as forest dwellers and those who did not follow Brahmanical norms or spoke non-Sanskritic languages were often labelled:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mlechchhas
Why: Brahmanical texts called such people mlechchhas and looked down on them. There was still exchange of ideas and beliefs with them.
Why not the others: (B) Gahapatis were household heads. (C) Kshatriyas were a varna within the system. (D) A gotra was a Brahmanical lineage unit.
Key point: The Brahmanical ideal of varna was never fully accepted by everyone.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: Mirabai, a Rajput princess from Merta in Marwar who was married into the Sisodia clan of Mewar, is believed to have recognised as her guru:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Raidas
Why: Tradition holds that Mirabai's guru was Raidas, a leatherworker. Choosing him was itself a defiance of caste norms.
Why not the others: (A) Kabir, (C) Chaitanya and (D) Shankaradeva are other saints. None is linked with her as guru.
Key point: Mirabai defied her husband's family and the norms of a wife's conduct, and her songs are still sung in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question: The sixteenth-century Portuguese writer Duarte Barbosa wrote a detailed account of trade and society in:
options: A) The Mughal court at Agra
C) Bengal and the eastern coast
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) South India
Why: Barbosa wrote a detailed account of trade and society in south India.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not the regions of his account.
Key point: Portuguese writers became important observers of the western and southern coasts after Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 into a Hindu merchant family in a village near the river Ravi, now known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Nankana Sahib
Why: Guru Nanak was born at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib, near the Ravi in present-day Pakistan.
Why not the others: (B) Kartarpur is the centre he set up later on the Ravi. (A) and (D) are linked with later Gurus.
Key point: Guru Nanak's hymns are in the Adi Granth Sahib, compiled by Guru Arjan.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question: In the early 1920s, the archaeologist who found seals at Harappa in layers that were definitely much older than Early Historic levels was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Daya Ram Sahni
Why: Daya Ram Sahni found seals at Harappa in the early 1920s. R.D. Banerji found similar seals at Mohenjodaro, and the two finds together showed that the sites belonged to one civilisation.
Why not the others: (A) Banerji worked at Mohenjodaro. (B) Cunningham, the first Director-General of the ASI, did not recognise how old Harappa was. (D) Wheeler excavated in the 1940s.
Key point: In 1924 John Marshall announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.sub_topic: Sources on Gandhi and the national movement
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Source)
(A) Fortnightly reports
(B) *Hind Swaraj*
(C) *Harijan*
(D) *An Autobiography*

List-II (Description)
(I) Gandhi's own account of his life, written in the 1920s
(II) A journal in which Gandhi published many of his writings
(III) Confidential reports by the Home Department on the political situation
(IV) A book written by Gandhi in 1909, criticising modern civilisation
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Fortnightly reports were the Home Department's confidential reports (III). *Hind Swaraj* (1909) attacked modern civilisation (IV). *Harijan* was one of Gandhi's journals (II), and *An Autobiography* told his life story (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two. (B) swaps *Hind Swaraj* and *Harijan*. (C) swaps *Harijan* and the autobiography.
Key point: Each source has its own bias. Police reports saw the movement through officials' eyes, and the autobiography is a selective memory.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about decisions in the Constituent Assembly:
(A) Subjects were divided into three lists: Union, State and Concurrent.
(B) The Assembly declared Hindi the national language of India.
(C) The Congress dominated the Assembly, holding about 82% of its seats.
(D) B.R. Ambedkar argued for a strong and united Centre.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A), (C) and (D) follow NCERT. The three lists, the dominance of the Congress, and Ambedkar's call for a strong Centre are all described there.
Why not the others: (B) is false. The Assembly made Hindi in Devanagari the official language, not the national language, with English continuing for fifteen years. Options (B), (C) and (D) include (B).
Key point: The partition violence persuaded many members that only a strong Centre could hold the country together.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: After months of working to restore peace between Hindus and Muslims, Mahatma Gandhi was shot dead in Delhi on:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 30 January 1948
Why: Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948 at his evening prayer meeting in Delhi.
Why not the others: (B) is Independence Day, (C) the day the Constitution came into force, and (D) would have been his 79th birthday.
Key point: In his last months Gandhi went to Noakhali, Bihar, Calcutta and Delhi to stop communal violence.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.sub_topic: Painter of The Relief of Lucknow
questions.question: The 1859 painting *The Relief of Lucknow*, which celebrated the British heroes who rescued those besieged at the Residency, was painted by ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Thomas Jones Barker
Why: Thomas Jones Barker painted *The Relief of Lucknow* in 1859. It shows Campbell, Outram and Havelock as heroes.
Why not the others: (A) Joseph Noel Paton painted *In Memoriam*. (B) Felice Beato was a photographer. (C) Raja Ravi Varma was a later Indian painter.
Key point: British pictures of 1857 showed revenge and rescue, while nationalist images later celebrated rebel leaders such as Rani Lakshmi Bai.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.sub_topic: Cause of the cotton boom in the Deccan
questions.question: The sudden demand for raw cotton from the Bombay Deccan in the early 1860s was caused by:
options: A) The opening of the Suez Canal
B) The end of the Permanent Settlement
C) A severe famine in Egypt
D) The outbreak of the Civil War in the USA
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The outbreak of the Civil War in the USA
Why: The American Civil War broke out in 1861. Raw cotton from America stopped reaching Britain, so British manufacturers turned to India.
Why not the others: (A) The Suez Canal opened in 1869. (B) is unrelated. (C) is not the cause NCERT gives.
Key point: When the war ended, the boom ended too, leaving ryots deep in debt and leading to the Deccan riots.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question: Recent studies of a skeleton found at Rakhigarhi have used archaeogenetics. This field is the study of:
options: A) Ancient DNA recovered from human remains
B) The chemical composition of Harappan pottery
C) The age of bricks measured from their size
D) Fossil pollen preserved in old lake beds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ancient DNA recovered from human remains
Why: Archaeogenetics studies ancient DNA, usually taken from skeletons, to learn about the ancestry and movement of past populations.
Why not the others: (B) is ceramic analysis. (C) is not a dating method. (D) is pollen analysis (palynology).
Key point: Archaeogenetics joins other scientific methods, such as the study of animal bones and plant remains, in reconstructing the Harappan past.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) Guru Nanak
(B) Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya
(C) Basavanna
(D) Appar, a Nayanar saint
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D), (C), (B), (A)
Why: Appar belongs to the early Nayanar period (about the seventh century). Basavanna lived in the twelfth century, Nizamuddin Auliya died in 1325, and Guru Nanak was born in 1469.
Why not the others: (A) puts Basavanna before Appar. (B) puts Nizamuddin before Basavanna. (C) puts Guru Nanak before Nizamuddin.
Key point: Bhakti in the Tamil region (sixth to ninth centuries) came well before the northern Sant tradition.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question: In the Assembly debates, the socialist peasant leader N.G. Ranga argued that the real minorities who needed protection were:
options: A) Religious groups such as Muslims, Sikhs and Christians
B) The poor and downtrodden, such as peasants and tribals
C) The princes, who were losing their states and privileges
D) Speakers of languages other than Hindi in the south
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The poor and downtrodden, such as peasants and tribals
Why: Ranga said that the real minorities were the masses, the poor and the downtrodden, who lacked the means to use the rights the Constitution would give them.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are other groups. Ranga's point was economic, not religious or linguistic.
Key point: Ranga wanted the Constitution to create conditions in which ordinary people could enjoy their rights.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question: François Bernier, who stayed in the Mughal empire from 1656 to 1668, was by profession a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Physician
Why: Bernier was a French physician, political philosopher and historian. He was closely associated with the Mughal court as physician to Prince Dara Shukoh.
Why not the others: (A) does not fit Bernier. (B) The French jeweller Tavernier traded in diamonds. (C) Jesuit priests such as Monserrate came to Akbar's court.
Key point: Bernier constantly compared India with Europe, often to show India as inferior.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.sub_topic: Harappan sites and their distinctive features
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Site)
(A) Harappa
(B) Mohenjodaro
(C) Kalibangan
(D) Dholavira

List-II (Feature)
(I) Evidence of a ploughed field
(II) Large water reservoirs cut into rock
(III) A large, tank-like structure in the Citadel known as the Great Bath
(IV) The first site found, badly damaged by brick robbers and railway builders
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Harappa was the first site found, and its bricks were carried away for railway lines (IV). The Great Bath is at Mohenjodaro (III). Kalibangan has the ploughed field (I), and Dholavira its water reservoirs (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Harappa and Mohenjodaro. (C) swaps Kalibangan and Dholavira. (D) swaps Harappa and Kalibangan.
Key point: Because Harappa was so badly damaged, Mohenjodaro is the best-known Harappan site.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.sub_topic: Places connected with the Buddha's life
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Place)
(A) Lumbini
(B) Bodh Gaya
(C) Sarnath
(D) Kusinagara

List-II (Event)
(I) First sermon
(II) Birth
(III) Passing away (mahaparinibbana)
(IV) Enlightenment
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: The Buddha was born at Lumbini (II), attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya (IV), gave his first sermon at Sarnath (I) and passed away at Kusinagara (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps Lumbini and Bodh Gaya. (C) swaps Bodh Gaya and Sarnath. (D) swaps Sarnath and Kusinagara.
Key point: All four places became sacred, and stupas and monasteries grew up at them.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Harappan script:
(A) The script remains undeciphered to this day.
(B) It was probably written from right to left, because some seals show wider spacing on the right and cramping on the left.
(C) It was alphabetic, with about fifty letters.
(D) Most inscriptions are very long, with over a hundred signs each.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) and (B) only
Why: (A) and (B) follow NCERT: the script is undeciphered and was probably written right to left.
Why not the others: (C) is false. The script was not alphabetic, because it has too many signs, somewhere between 375 and 400. (D) is false. Most inscriptions are short, and the longest has about 26 signs. Options (B), (C) and (D) each include a false statement.
Key point: Seals were used to stamp sealed bags of goods, which shows long-distance exchange.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Vijayanagara:
(A) The river Tungabhadra flows south-west and forms a natural basin around the city.
(B) The Kamalapuram tank, built in the fifteenth century, irrigated nearby fields and also fed the royal centre through a channel.
(C) The Hiriya canal drew water from a dam across the Tungabhadra and irrigated the valley between the sacred centre and the urban core.
(D) Abdur Razzaq noted that the city was enclosed by seven lines of fortification.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: (B), (C) and (D) follow NCERT. The tank fed fields and the royal centre, the Hiriya canal irrigated the valley, and Abdur Razzaq described seven lines of forts.
Why not the others: (A) is false, because the Tungabhadra flows north-east. Options (A) and (B) include (A), and option (C) leaves out the true statement (D).
Key point: The walls also enclosed fields and forests, so the city could survive a long siege.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question: James Prinsep, who deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi in 1838, was an officer in the ____ of the East India Company.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Mint
Why: Prinsep worked in the Company's mint. His decipherment opened up the reading of Ashokan inscriptions and gave a new direction to early Indian political history.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) were not his posts.
Key point: Most Ashokan inscriptions are in Prakrit and in the Brahmi script. Those in the northwest are in Kharosthi.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.sub_topic: Fatalist teacher of the Buddha's time
questions.question: Buddhist texts record the views of rival teachers. The view that everything is predetermined, so that neither the wise nor the fool can change the course of saṃsāra, is associated with:
options: B) Makkhali Gosala, of the Ajivikas
C) Vardhamana Mahavira, of the Jainas
D) Sariputta, a disciple of the Buddha
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Makkhali Gosala, of the Ajivikas
Why: Makkhali Gosala, a leader of the Ajivikas, held that everything was predetermined, so Ajivikas are often called fatalists.
Why not the others: (A) Ajita Kesakambalin taught that nothing survives death, a materialist (Lokayata) view. (C) Mahavira taught that action shapes the cycle of birth and rebirth. (D) Sariputta was a disciple of the Buddha.
Key point: The sixth century BCE was a time of debate among many thinkers, who moved from place to place in kutagarashalas and groves.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.sub_topic: Incorrectly matched Harappan site and present-day region
questions.question: Identify the incorrectly matched pair of a Harappan site and its present-day location:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Lothal – Sindh
Why: Lothal is in Gujarat, not Sindh. It lies near the Gulf of Khambhat and was a centre of bead-making.
Why not the others: (A) Dholavira is in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat. (B) Kalibangan is in Rajasthan. (C) Rakhigarhi is in Haryana.
Key point: Mohenjodaro, not Lothal, is the major Harappan city in Sindh.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about rumours and beliefs in 1857:
(A) A rumour spread that the new cartridges were greased with the fat of cows and pigs.
(B) It was rumoured that bone dust of cows and pigs had been mixed into flour sold in the market.
(C) The rebels' proclamations appealed only to Muslims and ignored Hindus.
(D) A prophecy said that British rule would end on the centenary of the battle of Plassey.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) follow NCERT. The cartridge and flour rumours spread fear of a plot against caste and religion, and the Plassey centenary prophecy fell in 1857.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Proclamations, such as those issued in Bahadur Shah's name, appealed to Hindus and Muslims alike to fight together. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include (C).
Key point: Rumours spread because they matched deeper fears about British policies on reform and conversion.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: The Vijayanagara kings depended on horses imported from Arabia and Central Asia for their cavalry. The local merchants in this trade were known as ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Kudirai chettis
Why: Horse merchants were called kudirai chettis. The horse trade was at first controlled by Arab traders and later by the Portuguese.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are other trading groups. (D) were military commanders.
Key point: Rivalry with the Deccan Sultanates over the trade in horses was one reason for wars.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.sub_topic: Terms in sources on early states
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Shreni
(B) Gahapati
(C) Agrahara
(D) Gana or sangha

List-II (Meaning)
(I) The owner, master or head of a household
(II) A state ruled by a group of men, not by a single king
(III) A guild or association of crafts producers and merchants
(IV) Land granted to brahmanas, usually exempt from land revenue
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: A shreni was a guild (III), a gahapati the head of a household (I), an agrahara land granted to brahmanas (IV), and a gana or sangha an oligarchy (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps shreni and gahapati. (B) swaps agrahara and gana. (C) swaps gahapati and agrahara.
Key point: Some mahajanapadas were ruled by kings, while others, the ganas or sanghas, were oligarchies. The Buddha and Mahavira belonged to such ganas.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: Gandhi represented the Congress at the Second Round Table Conference in London in late 1931. Why did the conference fail?
options: A) The British government refused to allow any Indian leader to attend or speak at its sessions
B) Gandhi walked out on the first day so that he could begin the Salt March
C) The Muslim League, the princes and Ambedkar disputed Gandhi's claim to speak for all India
D) The conference was called off because the Quit India Movement had begun
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The Muslim League, the princes and Ambedkar disputed Gandhi's claim to speak for all India
Why: Gandhi claimed the Congress represented all India. The Muslim League, the princes and B.R. Ambedkar, who claimed to speak for the depressed classes, challenged that claim, and the conference ended without result.
Why not the others: (A) Indian leaders did attend. (B) The Salt March came before the conference, in 1930. (D) Quit India came in 1942.
Key point: Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the depressed classes, which Gandhi opposed.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.sub_topic: Auction of the Burdwan raja's estates
questions.question: In 1797 an auction was held of several mahals held by the Raja of Burdwan. Many of the purchasers turned out to be:
options: A) British officers of the East India Company
B) The raja's own servants and agents
D) Moneylenders from the Bombay Deccan
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The raja's own servants and agents
Why: The raja's own agents bought many of the lands in fictitious sales. He kept control of his estates while appearing to have lost them.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not the buyers NCERT describes.
Key point: Zamindars used such tricks because the revenue demand under the Permanent Settlement was high and inflexible.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about al-Biruni:
(A) He wrote the *Kitab-ul-Hind* in Arabic.
(B) He was born in Morocco and crossed North Africa to reach India.
(C) He translated several Sanskrit works, including Patanjali's work on grammar, into Arabic.
(D) He held that a system like caste had no parallel anywhere else in the world.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A) and (C) only
Why: (A) and (C) follow NCERT. He wrote in Arabic and translated Sanskrit works into Arabic.
Why not the others: (B) is false, because al-Biruni was born in Khwarizm in present-day Uzbekistan. It was Ibn Battuta who came from Morocco. (D) is false, because he compared caste with the four social categories of ancient Persia. Options (A), (B) and (D) each include a false statement.
Key point: Al-Biruni accepted the Brahmanical description of caste but rejected the notion of pollution.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question: Ashoka appointed special officers, known as ____, to spread the message of dhamma.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Dhamma mahamatta
Why: Ashoka's inscriptions say that he appointed dhamma mahamattas to spread the message of dhamma.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are Gupta-period official titles, all held by Harisena, the poet of the Prayaga prashasti. None was an Ashokan officer of dhamma.
Key point: Ashoka's dhamma included respect for elders, generosity to brahmanas and renouncers, and good treatment of slaves and servants.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II according to the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras.

List-I (Varna)
(A) Brahmanas
(B) Kshatriyas
(C) Vaishyas
(D) Shudras

List-II (Prescribed occupation)
(I) Serving the three "higher" varnas
(II) Agriculture, pastoralism and trade
(III) Warfare, protecting people and administering justice
(IV) Studying and teaching the Vedas, performing sacrifices
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Brahmanas were to study and teach the Vedas (IV), Kshatriyas to fight and protect (III), Vaishyas to farm, keep cattle and trade (II), and Shudras to serve the higher three (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two. (B) swaps Kshatriyas and Vaishyas. (D) swaps Vaishyas and Shudras.
Key point: The Brahmanas tried to enforce these norms by claiming they were divinely ordained, by advising kings, and by persuading people.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question: Jaina monks and nuns took vows to abstain from killing, stealing and lying, to observe celibacy and to abstain from possessing property. How many vows were these?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Five
Why: These are the five great vows of Jaina monks and nuns.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are the wrong number.
Key point: The Jaina emphasis on ahimsa extends to all living beings, including plants and insects.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: In the Vijayanagara empire, the amara-nayakas were:
options: A) Military commanders given territories to govern by the raya
B) Priests who managed the Virupaksha temple and its lands
C) Merchants who brought horses from Arabia and Central Asia
D) Village headmen who measured land and fixed the revenue
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Military commanders given territories to govern by the raya
Why: Amara-nayakas were military commanders who received territories from the raya. They collected taxes, kept horses and elephants for the king, and sent him tribute.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) describe other groups.
Key point: The amara-nayaka system was a major political innovation. It drew on the iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: The Champaran campaign of 1917, in which Gandhi sought security of tenure and the freedom to grow crops of their choice for indigo peasants, took place in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Bihar
Why: Champaran is in Bihar. Gandhi went there to help peasants forced to grow indigo for European planters.
Why not the others: (A) Gujarat was the scene of Kheda and the Ahmedabad mill strike. (C) and (D) are not the place of this campaign.
Key point: Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad (1917–18) gave Gandhi a reputation as a nationalist with sympathy for the poor.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.sub_topic: Chronology of events leading to 1857 in Awadh
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) The annexation of Awadh
(B) Awadh is made to accept the subsidiary alliance
(C) The battle of Plassey
(D) The outbreak of the revolt at Meerut
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (B), (A), (D)
Why: Plassey was fought in 1757, Awadh accepted the subsidiary alliance in 1801, Awadh was annexed in 1856, and the revolt broke out at Meerut in 1857.
Why not the others: (A) puts the subsidiary alliance before Plassey. (B) puts the annexation before the alliance. (D) puts the revolt before the annexation.
Key point: Awadh lost its army under the subsidiary alliance and its nawab under the annexation, so grievances built up over half a century.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

Abu'l Fazl's *Ain-i Akbari* explains how the Mughal state under Akbar assessed land for revenue. Land was first classified by how regularly it was cultivated. Polaj was land cultivated every year for each crop and never allowed to lie fallow. Parauti was land left out of cultivation for a time so that it could recover its strength. Chachar was land that had lain fallow for three or four years, and banjar was land left uncultivated for five years or more.

For polaj and parauti, each of the good, middling and bad kinds was measured, and the produce of the three was added together. One-third of this average produce was taken as the state's demand. Chachar and banjar lands were brought back into cultivation on lighter terms, with the demand rising year by year.

The *Ain* also separated the amount assessed (jama) from the amount actually collected (hasil). Historians value the text for its range of detail, but they also note its limits. Its totals do not always add up, its data are uneven from province to province, and its lists of prices and wages come mostly from the region around Agra, the capital.

Question: According to the passage, land that was cultivated every year for each crop and never left fallow was called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Polaj
Why: The passage defines polaj as land "cultivated every year for each crop and never allowed to lie fallow".
Why not the others: (A) Parauti was left out of cultivation for a while to recover. (C) Chachar had been fallow for three or four years. (D) Banjar had been uncultivated for five years or more.
Key point: The four categories run from most to least regularly cultivated: polaj → parauti → chachar → banjar.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

Abu'l Fazl's *Ain-i Akbari* explains how the Mughal state under Akbar assessed land for revenue. Land was first classified by how regularly it was cultivated. Chachar and banjar lands were brought back into cultivation on lighter terms, with the demand rising year by year.

Its totals do not always add up, its data are uneven from province to province, and its lists of prices and wages come mostly from the region around Agra, the capital.

Question: What separated chachar land from banjar land in the *Ain*'s classification?
options: A) Chachar was irrigated by canals, while banjar depended on rain
B) Chachar was held by zamindars, while banjar belonged to the state
C) Chachar grew cash crops, while banjar grew only food grains
D) Chachar had lain fallow for three or four years, banjar for five or more
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Chachar had lain fallow for three or four years, banjar for five or more
Why: The classification is by the length of fallow: chachar three or four years, banjar five years or more.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) bring in irrigation, ownership and crop type, which the passage does not use to classify land.
Key point: Lands that had lain fallow longer were brought back on lighter, rising demands to encourage cultivation.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.sub_topic: Share of produce taken as revenue
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

Abu'l Fazl's *Ain-i Akbari* explains how the Mughal state under Akbar assessed land for revenue. Land was first classified by how regularly it was cultivated. Polaj was land cultivated every year for each crop and never allowed to lie fallow. Parauti was land left out of cultivation for a time so that it could recover its strength. Chachar was land that had lain fallow for three or four years, and banjar was land left uncultivated for five years or more.

For polaj and parauti, each of the good, middling and bad kinds was measured, and the produce of the three was added together. One-third of this average produce was taken as the state's demand. Chachar and banjar lands were brought back into cultivation on lighter terms, with the demand rising year by year.

The *Ain* also separated the amount assessed (jama) from the amount actually collected (hasil). Historians value the text for its range of detail, but they also note its limits. Its totals do not always add up, its data are uneven from province to province, and its lists of prices and wages come mostly from the region around Agra, the capital.

Question: How was the state's demand fixed for polaj and parauti land, according to the passage?
options: A) As one-third of the average produce of good, middling and bad land
B) As one-half of the produce of the best land in the village
C) As a fixed cash sum that never changed, whatever the harvest
D) As one-fourth of the produce, collected only in kind
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) As one-third of the average produce of good, middling and bad land
Why: The produce of the three kinds of land was added and averaged, and one-third of this average was the state's demand.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) give the wrong share. (C) is not in the passage, because the demand depended on assessed produce.
Key point: Averaging good, middling and bad land made the assessment fit the actual productivity of the area.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.sub_topic: A limitation of the Ain's data
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

Abu'l Fazl's *Ain-i Akbari* explains how the Mughal state under Akbar assessed land for revenue. Land was first classified by how regularly it was cultivated. Polaj was land cultivated every year for each crop and never allowed to lie fallow. Parauti was land left out of cultivation for a time so that it could recover its strength. Chachar was land that had lain fallow for three or four years, and banjar was land left uncultivated for five years or more.

For polaj and parauti, each of the good, middling and bad kinds was measured, and the produce of the three was added together. One-third of this average produce was taken as the state's demand. Chachar and banjar lands were brought back into cultivation on lighter terms, with the demand rising year by year.

The *Ain* also separated the amount assessed (jama) from the amount actually collected (hasil). Historians value the text for its range of detail, but they also note its limits. Its totals do not always add up, its data are uneven from province to province, and its lists of prices and wages come mostly from the region around Agra, the capital.

Question: Which of the following is a limitation of the *Ain-i Akbari* noted in the passage?
options: A) It was written long after Akbar's death, from memory
B) It ignores land revenue and deals only with court ceremony
C) Its price and wage lists come mostly from the region around Agra
D) It records only the amount collected, never the amount assessed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Its price and wage lists come mostly from the region around Agra
Why: The passage says the lists of prices and wages "come mostly from the region around Agra". Totals that do not add up and uneven provincial data are its other limits.
Why not the others: (A) The *Ain* was written in Akbar's reign. (B) Land revenue is its main concern here. (D) It records both jama and hasil.
Key point: The *Ain* gives the view from the imperial centre, so historians check it against regional sources.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

Abu'l Fazl's *Ain-i Akbari* explains how the Mughal state under Akbar assessed land for revenue. Land was first classified by how regularly it was cultivated. Polaj was land cultivated every year for each crop and never allowed to lie fallow. Parauti was land left out of cultivation for a time so that it could recover its strength. Chachar was land that had lain fallow for three or four years, and banjar was land left uncultivated for five years or more.

For polaj and parauti, each of the good, middling and bad kinds was measured, and the produce of the three was added together. One-third of this average produce was taken as the state's demand. Chachar and banjar lands were brought back into cultivation on lighter terms, with the demand rising year by year.

The *Ain* also separated the amount assessed (jama) from the amount actually collected (hasil). Historians value the text for its range of detail, but they also note its limits. Its totals do not always add up, its data are uneven from province to province, and its lists of prices and wages come mostly from the region around Agra, the capital.

Question: Which conclusion follows most directly from the way land was classified and assessed in the passage?
options: A) The state wanted to take exactly the same amount from every village, whatever its land was like
B) The state graded its demand by how regularly land was cultivated and drew fallow land back into use
C) The state intended to leave fallow land outside the revenue system permanently, taxing only polaj
D) The state assessed land mainly on the basis of the caste and status of the cultivator who held it
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The state graded its demand by how regularly land was cultivated and drew fallow land back into use
Why: Regularly cultivated land paid a third of average produce, while long-fallow land came back on lighter, rising terms. The demand was graded by land use, and cultivation was encouraged to spread.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts the different categories. (C) contradicts the lighter terms meant to bring fallow land back into use. (D) Caste plays no part in the passage.
Key point: Mughal revenue policy aimed both at collecting revenue and at extending cultivation.
